title: 1  Linear regression …
2  Binary Cross Entropy
text:
2.1 If you’re in a hurry :
The binary cross-entropy is the loss function that we use most of the time when performing binary classification.
The binary cross-entropy (for a single sample): \[
\ell(y,\hat{y}) = -\bigl[y\log(\hat{y}) + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})\bigr]
\]
For a dataset of N samples:
\[
\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl[y_i\log(\hat{y}_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{y}_i)\bigr]
\]

title: 2  Binary Cross Entropy
section: 2.2 Where the f does it comes from ?
text:
2.2 Where the f does it comes from ?
If you know basic statistical inference, this follows directly from the log-likelihood of the binomial distribution.
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),\quad Y_i\in\{0,1\},\; i=1,\dots,n,\\[4pt]
&\text{so }P(Y_i=y_i\mid p)=p^{y_i}(1-p)^{1-y_i}.\\[6pt]
&\text{For independent samples }y=(y_1,\dots,y_n),\text{ the likelihood is}\\[4pt]
&\quad L(p\mid y)=P(Y=y\mid p)=\prod_{i=1}^n p^{y_i}(1-p)^{1-y_i}
= p^{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i}\,(1-p)^{\,n-\sum_{i=1}^n y_i}.\\[6pt]
&\text{The log-likelihood is}\\[4pt]
&\quad \ell(p\mid y)=\log L(p\mid y)
= \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\Big)\log p + \Big(n-\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\Big)\log(1-p).\\[6pt]
&\text{Taking the negative log-likelihood (per-sample average) gives the binary cross-entropy:}\\[4pt]
&\quad -\frac{1}{n}\,\ell(p\mid y)
= -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[y_i\log p + (1-y_i)\log(1-p)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]






Note

title: 3  Sigmoid function
text:
A sigmoid function is any mathematical function whose graph has a characteristic S-shaped (sigmoid) curve. (Source: Wikipedia)

Sigmoid functions are commonly used as activation functions in neural networks. Especially for output layers,because their range is typically bounded between 0 and 1, making them convenient for interpreting outputs as probabilities.
Note: Sigmoid functions are not necessarily probability density functions (PDFs). Rather, many sigmoids map real inputs to the interval (0, 1) and can be interpreted as probabilities or as the cumulative distribution shape of some underlying process. PDFs integrate to 1 over their domain and usually take values \(\geq 0\), so the terms are different.
The most widely used sigmoid is the logistic function especially in binary classification:
\[
f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}
\]



Sigmoid function

title: 4  Dense / Linear layer
text:
All of these refer to the same core concept: a fully connected (dense) layer that implements an affine transform followed by an optional nonlinearity. It’s the basic building block of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), essentially “glorified linear regression” if you had the activation function.
Mathematical form:
\[
y = f(xA^\top + b)
\] where:

\(x\) is the input ,
\(A\) is the weight matrix,
\(b\) is the bias vector,
\(f\) is the activation function,
\(y\) is the output.

Common API names:

TensorFlow / Keras: tf.keras.layers.Dense
PyTorch: torch.nn.Linear
JAX / Flax (and similar libs): nnx.Linear (or flax.linen.Dense)

Typical behavior

Input/output shapes: if input is (batch, in_features) and layer has out_features, then \(A\) is (out_features, in_features)
Bias: optional; if present, added per output unit.
Initialization: frameworks provide sensible defaults (e.g., Glorot/Xavier, Kaiming) that affect training dynamics.
Use cases: hidden layers in MLPs, final classification/regression heads, linear projections in attention, embeddings projection, etc.

Derivative useful facts:

Parameter count: in_features * out_features + (out_features if bias)
Computation per forward pass: O(batch * in_features * out_features)

title: 5  Convolutional layers
text:
Convolutional layers (Conv2D) implement a local, weight-sharing affine map over spatial neighborhoods and are the core building block of CNNs. Practically, most deep‑learning libraries implement the operation as a 2D cross‑correlation (no kernel flip), not the mathematical convolution.

This is roughly the operation used by torch.nn.Conv2d, keras.layers.Conv2D, and flax.linen.Conv (they differ in API and default conventions but implement the same cross‑correlation‑based convolutional layer).
You can find more beautiful visualisations here
I won’t dive into more details because there’s A LOT of stuff to say about CNN but I will try to update this page later.

title: 6  RNN
text:
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are used for sequential data — signals, speech, text, financial time series where past values influence future ones. Their development is tightly linked to natural language processing.






Note



If you want a compact lecture, watch the MIT Intro to Deep Learning segment on RNNs. For a structured, rigorous treatment, see the d2l.ai chapters on RNN. This writeup aims to be a primer for both.



6.0.1 Elevator pitch
Think of autoregressive models from statistics: predict the next value mainly from past observations. Given a sequence \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\) and observations up to time \(t-1\), we want \[
\mathbb{E}\big(x_t \mid x_{t-1},\dots,x_1\big).
\]
A naive stats‑101 approach is linear regression, but that has practical issues: as time advances the number of predictors grows, and most interesting signals are nonlinear.
So how can we improve this first idea ? :

Fixed sliding window (use the last K values).
Instead of using a growing number of past values, use a fixed-size window of the last K observations (e.g., 2, 3, 5) as predictors for regression, or compute a summary (like the mean) over that window.
Compress past into a summary statistic (mean, moving average).
Collapsing the history into a single summary (mean, median, moving average, etc.) produces a fixed-size predictor regardless of sequence length, avoiding the predictor-scaling problem.
Combine both (rolling averages, exponentially weighted stats).
Use a fixed window plus a summary computed over that window (or an exponential weighting of all past observations) to get both locality and smoothed long-term information.



6.0.2 Latent autoregressive view
If we compress the past into a fixed‑size summary (a latent state) and use that to predict the next value, we get a latent autoregressive model. The latent state is not directly observed.
Write the model as \[
\hat{x}_t = P(x_t \mid h_t),
\] with the state updated recurrently, for example \[
h_t = g(h_{t-1},\, x_{t-1}).
\]
(The hat denotes a predicted quantity; un‑hatted symbols are observed.)



Visual summary that will make sense later by d2l.ai


This formulation: a state that summarizes the past and is iteratively updated is the core idea behind RNNs.


6.0.3 How this maps to RNNs

\(h_t\) is the hidden state (fixed-dimensional vector).

\(g\) is a parametric update (for simple RNNs, \(g\) is an affine map followed by a nonlinearity).

The output model \(P\) can be a simple linear layer or a more complex head (softmax for language, Gaussian for regression, etc.).

A simple vanilla RNN usually looks like this: \[
h_t = \phi\big(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_{t-1} + b\big),
\qquad
\hat{y}_t = W_y h_t + c,
\] where \(\phi\) is a nonlinearity (tanh, ReLU), and \(W_h,W_x,W_y\) are learned weight matrices and \(b,c\) are optional biases.
If you have experience with Markov models, you can link them to a transition probability matrix. It was never written explicitly until now, but assuming that we can make a solid prediction by only looking at \(K\) values in the past is essentially assuming the process we’re interested in is a Markov process of order \(K\). This link is discussed in greater detail in the d2l.ai course.


6.0.4 Practical considerations and modern practice
RNNs are largely superseded in many applications, but still conceptually important.

Vanilla RNNs suffer from vanishing/exploding gradients for long dependencies. Gated architectures (LSTM, GRU) mitigate this with learned gates that control information flow.
For many NLP and sequence tasks, Transformer architectures have largely supplanted RNNs because they model long‑range dependencies more effectively and parallelize better.



6.0.5 Further reading/watching
As I said in the beginning, this is mainly intended as an introduction to RNN. I highly encourage you to watch this lecture MIT Intro to Deep Learning segment on RNNs and read the d2l.ai chapters on RNN to get a more formal understanding.

title: 7  Filtering
text:
7.1 Type of filters
We observe a time-varying quantity x(t), but measurements are imperfect — what we actually record is y(t), which equals the true signal plus an error term:
\[y(t)=x(t)+b(t).\]
Recovering x(t) from the noisy observation y(t) is called filtering — i.e., designing a method that suppresses the noise b(t) while retaining the desired signal x(t).
Usually we think of filters in two main groups: - Linear filters - Non-linear filters

title: 7  Filtering
text:
7.1.1 Why are we interested in linear filters ?
If the system is linear and time‑invariant, its action on any input is completely characterized by its impulse response h(t) (or equivalently its transfer function H(s)/H(ω)). Convolving the measured signal with h gives the system’s output or an estimate of the underlying signal:
\[\tilde{x}(t)=y(t)\ast h(t).\]
Using linearity and y(t)=x(t)+b(t):
\[\tilde{x}(t)=(x(t)+b(t))\ast h(t)=x(t)\ast h(t)+b(t)\ast h(t).\]
Ideally, \(b(t)\ast h(t) = 0\)


7.1.2 Link with the fourier transform
The fourier transform turns the convolution into a simple product. \[ TF(y(t)*h(t)) = Y(f) H(f)\]

title: 7  Filtering
section: 7.2 Energy and the energy spectral density
text:
7.2 Energy and the energy spectral density

For a finite‑energy signal x(t) the total energy is defined as \[
E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^{2}dt.
\]

Let \(\hat{x}(f)\) be the Fourier transform of \(x(t)\) (frequency (f) in Hz).

By Parseval’s theorem, \[
E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^{2}dt=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\hat{x}(f)|^{2}df.
\] The nonnegative function \(|\hat{x}(f)|^{2}\) is called the energy spectral density (ESD) of \((x(t)\).

For any band \([f_1,f_2]\), \[
  \int_{f_1}^{f_2}|\hat{x}(f)|^{2}\,df
\] equals the energy contained in that frequency band.
Think of the total energy E as a cake. The Fourier transform splits the cake across frequencies; \(|\hat{x}(f)|^{2}\) is the slice size (energy per unit frequency) at frequency f.
Thus \(|\hat{x}(f)|^{2}\) is the energy contribution around frequency f,integrating it over a band tells you how much energy that band carries.
\[
\text{(ESD)} S_{xx}(f) = |\hat{x}(f)|^2
\]

Using the Wiener-Khintchine theorem: the ESD can be defined as the fourier transform of the autocorrelation signal:

\[ S_{xx}(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} R_{xx}(\tau)e^{-2 \pi i f \tau} d\tau\]






Why is the autocorrelation function only a function of the lag \(\tau\)



For a (complex) stochastic process X(t) the general autocorrelation is \[
R_{XX}(t_1,t_2)=\mathbb{E}\big[X(t_1)\,\overline{X(t_2)}\big],
\] which a priori depends on both times t1 and t2.
If X(t) is wide-sense stationary (WSS) then by definition:

The mean \(\mu(X(t))=E[X(t)]\) is constant in time,
the autocorrelation is invariant under time shifts.

Time-shift invariance means: for any real shift \(\Delta\), \[
R_{XX}(t_1+\Delta,t_2+\Delta)=R_{XX}(t_1,t_2).
\] Fix any pair \((t_1,t_2)\).
Choose \(\Delta = −t_2\). Then \[
R_{XX}(t_1,t_2)=R_{XX}(t_1-t_2,0).
\]
Thus the value of \(R_{XX}\) at \((t_1,t_2)\) equals its value at \((t_1−t_2,0)\); it depends only on the difference \(t_1−t_2\), not on the absolute times.
Writing \(\tau = t_1−t_2\) gives the single-argument form \[
R_{XX}(\tau)=\mathbb{E}\big[X(t+\tau)\,\overline{X(t)}\big],
\] which is independent of the particular t chosen because of the shift invariance.
If the process is zero-mean (centered), the autocovariance \(K_{XX}\) equals the autocorrelation \(R_{XX}\), so the same reduction to a single-argument function holds: \[
K_{XX}(t_1,t_2)=K_{XX}(\tau)=R_{XX}(\tau).
\] In short: WSS implies time-translation invariance of second-order statistics. That invariance forces the two-time function \(R_{XX}(t_1,t_2)\) to depend only on the time difference \(\tau = t_1−t_2\).

title: 8  The Wiener Filter
text:
8.1 Wiener filtering
The Wiener filter is a classical signal-processing method developed by Norbert Wiener in the 1940s. The objective is to reconstruct a target signal \(x(t)\) from a noisy observation: \[
y(t)=x(t)+b(t),
\] where \(b(t)\) is additive noise.

title: 8  The Wiener Filter
text:
8.2 How it works ?
The problem is formulated as an optimisation problem where we’re looking for h such as:
\[
\tilde{x}(t)=(h*y)(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} h(u)y(t-u)du
\] is as close as possible to the original signal (x(t)).
The measure of proximity/distance is the mean squared error.
\[
J=\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(x(t)-\tilde{x}(t)\big)^2\Big].
\]
The goal is to find \(h(t)\) that minimizes \(J\) or mathematically:
\[
\min_{h(\cdot)}J(h)=\min_{h(\cdot)}\;\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(x(t)-\!(h*y)(t)\big)^2\Big]
\]

title: 8  The Wiener Filter
text:
8.3 Solving the optimization problem
If a solution exist, it’s necessarily a local minimum so we can find possible solutions by derivating the J function.
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial h} = 2\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(x(t)-(h*y)(t)\big)
\frac{\partial}{\partial h}\big(x(t)-(h*y)(t)\big)\Big]
\]
Since \(x(t)\) does not depend on \(h\) and \((h*y)(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(u)y(t-u)du\), the functional derivative is
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial h(u)}\big(x(t)-(h*y)(t)\big)
= -y(t-u).
\]
Therefore the Gateaux derivative (set to zero for optimality) is \[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial h(v)}= -2\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(x(t)-(h*y)(t)\big)\,y(t-v)\Big] = 0,
\qquad\forall v,
\] which is the orthogonality condition.
This condition can be understood intuitively by the idea that our estimation error should not be correlated to the signal we’re observing.

title: 8  The Wiener Filter
text:
8.4 Frequency-domain formulation
In the frequency domain the problem simplifies.
Our initial equation is: \[
Y(f)=X(f)+B(f)
\] With \(Y\) the observation,\(X\) the signal,\(B\) the noise, all in the fourier domain.
We’re looking for \[\tilde{X}(f)=H(f)Y(f)\]
Define the power spectral densities (PSDs): \[
S_{xx}(f)=\mathbb{E}\big[|X(f)|^2\big],\qquad S_{yy}(f)=S_{xx}(f)+S_{bb}(f).
\]






Why \(S_{yy}(f)=S_{xx}(f)+S_{bb}(f)\) ?



Start from \(Y(f)=X(f)+B(f)\). By definition the (one-sided) power spectral density is the expected squared magnitude:
\[S_{yy}(f)=\mathbb{E}\big[|Y(f)|^2\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[Y(f)\overline{Y(f)}\big].\] Substitute \(Y(f) = X(f) + B(f)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{yy}(f)
&=\mathbb{E}\big[(X(f)+B(f))\overline{(X(f)+B(f))}\big]\\
&=\mathbb{E}\big[X(f)\overline{X(f)}\big]
+\mathbb{E}\big[B(f)\overline{B(f)}\big]
+\mathbb{E}\big[X(f)\overline{B(f)}\big]
+\mathbb{E}\big[B(f)\overline{X(f)}\big].
\end{aligned}
\]
If X and B are uncorrelated (or independent) then the cross terms vanish: \[\mathbb{E}\big[X(f)\overline{B(f)}\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[B(f)\overline{X(f)}\big]=0.\] Thus \[S_{yy}(f)=\mathbb{E}[|X(f)|^2]+\mathbb{E}[|B(f)|^2]=S_{xx}(f)+S_{bb}(f).\]


The optimal solution is the frequency-domain Wiener filter: \[
H(f)=\frac{S_{xx}(f)}{S_{yy}(f)}=\frac{S_{xx}(f)}{S_{xx}(f)+S_{bb}(f)} = \frac{1}{1+\frac{S_{bb}}{S_{xx}}}
\]






Why \(H(f)=\frac{S_{xx}(f)}{S_{yy}(f)}\) ?



To figure this out, we need to rewrite the optimization equation in the fourier domain
\[
\begin{aligned}
J(f)
&= \mathbb{E}\Big[\big(X(f)-\tilde{X}(f)\big)^2\Big] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\Big[\big(X(f)-H(f)Y(f)\big)^2\Big] \\
&= \mathbb{E}\Big[X(f)^2 - 2 X(f)H(f)Y(f) + \big(H(f)Y(f)\big)^2\Big]\\
&= \mathbb{E}\Big[X(f)^2\Big] + 2H(f)\mathbb{E}\Big[X(f)Y(f)\Big] + H(f)^2\mathbb{E}\Big[Y(f)^2\Big]\\
\end{aligned}
\]
Now differentiating this equation leads to:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial J}{\partial H(f)}= 0 \Leftrightarrow \\
&2 S_{xy} + 2 H(f)S_{yy}=0
&H(f) = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}}
\end{aligned}
\]
Now \(S_{xy}\) is slightly different than \(S_{xx}\) at first glance but they actually match because we assume the noise is uncorrelated to the signal.
\[
S_{xy} = \mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X(X+B)]= \mathbb{E}[X^2] + \mathbb{E}[XB] = E[X^2] = S_{xx}
\]

title: 10  Exercice 1
text:
Note



I chose to keep the exercies in french for my classmates.


On souhaite à partir d’une observation du processus aléatoire \(y(t)\) résultant de la somme de deux signaux décorrélés \(x(t)\) et \(b(t)\) de densités spectrales de puissance respectives \(S_{xx}(f)\) et \(S_{bb}(f)\) estimer le processus aléatoire de \(x(t)\) par filtrage.

Proposer et justifier le choix du filtre approprié à cette application

\(y(t) = x(t)+b(t)\)
On a supposé que le bruit est décorrélé du signal x. En supposant que le signal x est stationnaire au deuxième degré et centré, le filtre de Wiener de débruitage semble adapté.

Donner l’expression du gain complexe (réponse en fréquence) du filtre optimal en fonction des densités spectrales de puissance des deux signaux \(x(t)\) et \(b(t)\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
H(f) = \frac{S_{xx}}{S_{yy}} \\
H(f) = \frac{S_{xx}}{S_{xx}+S_{bb}} \\
H(f) = \frac{1}{1+\frac{S_{bb}}{S_{xx}}} \\
\end{aligned}
\]

Si \(b(t)\) est un bruit blanc,centré et de variance \(N_0=1\) et \(x(t)\) est stationnaire au second ordre,centré, réel,de densitéé spectrale de puissance : \[
S_{xx}(f) = \frac{1}{4 \pi^2f^2+15}
\]

Calculer et tracer la réponse impulsionnelle du filtre; On donne la transformée de Fourier : \(TF(e^{-a|t|})= \frac{2a}{4 \pi^2f^2+a^2}\) , \(a\) étant un réel strictement positif.
L’idée principale de cette question est que l’auto-corrélation du bruit/la dsp est égale à la variance pour le bruit blanc par définition.
La variance est \(\mathbb{E}[b^2]=1=S_{bb}\)
De cette observation suit que :
\[
H(f) = \frac{1}{q \pi^2f^2+16}
\]
Or d’après l’énoncé : \(TF(e^{-a|t|})= \frac{2a}{4 \pi^2f^2+a^2}\)
Ainsi, par identification : Pour \(a=4\), \[\frac{1}{8}TF(e^{-4|t|})=H(f)\]
D’où la réponse impulsionnelle: \[
TF^{-1}(H(f))(t) =h(t) = \frac{1}{8}e^{-4|t|}
\]


import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set(style="whitegrid")
t = np.linspace(-2, 2, 1001)
f = 0.125 * np.exp(-4 * np.abs(t))
peaks = [0]
vals = [0.125]
annot_x = np.array([-1, 0, 1])
annot_y = 0.125 * np.exp(-4 * np.abs(annot_x))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4))
ax.plot(t, f, color="#1f77b4", lw=2)
ax.fill_between(t, f, color="#1f77b4", alpha=0.12)
ax.scatter(peaks, vals, color="crimson", zorder=5)
ax.scatter(annot_x, annot_y, color="darkorange", zorder=5)
for x,y,label in zip(annot_x,annot_y,[r"$t=-1,\ f=\frac{1}{8}e^{-4}$", r"$t=0,\ f=\frac{1}{8}$", r"$t=1,\ f=\frac{1}{8}e^{-4}$"]):
    ax.annotate(label, xy=(x,y), xytext=(x, y+0.02), ha="center", color="black", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("t")
ax.set_ylabel("f(t)")
ax.set_title(r"$f(t)=\frac{1}{8}e^{-4|t|}$")
ax.set_xlim(-2,2)
ax.set_ylim(0,0.14)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Calculer et tracer la fonction d’autocorrélation du signal x(t). En déduire la puissance du signal.

L’idée principale de cette question est dd’utiliser le théorème de Wiener-Kintchine qui établit un lien entre l’autocorrélation qu’uon cherche et la dsp qu’on connait.
\[
TF[R_{xx}(\tau)] = S_{xx}(f)]
\] Donc
\[
R_{xx}(\tau) = TF^{-1}[S_{xx}(f)]
\]
En procédant par identification, on peut retrouver:
\[
R_{xx}(\tau) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{15}}e^{- \sqrt{15}|\tau|}
\]
Pour trouver la puissance du signal \(x(t)\) on utilise encore le théorème de Wiener-Kintchine et on l’évalue en 0.
Par défintion, \[
P_x = \int S_{xx}(f)df
\]
Or
\[
R_{xx}(\tau) = \int S_{xx}e^{j 2 \pi f \tau} df
\]
En \(\tau =0\), l’exponentiel disparait et on retrouve que :
\[
P_x = R_{xx}(0)
\]

title: 11  Exercice 2
11  Exercice 2
text:
11.2 Question 3
Afin d’évaluer la performance théorique dd’un tel filtre, on rélaise le traitement suivant:

On peut remarquer que si en sortie du filtre nous avons \(w(t)=e(t)\) (estimation parfaite, alors \(z(t)= e(t)-w(t)=0\) On définit le facteur de qualité par : \[
Q = \frac{S_{ee}(f)}{S_{zz}(f)}
\]
On se propose par la suite de calculer Q. Le filtre sera d’autant plus efficace que \(Q >>1\)

11.2.1 3-1) Exprimez la fonction d’auto-corrélation statistique \(R_{zz}(\tau) = \mathbb{E}[z(t)z*(t-\tau)]\) de \(z(t)=e(t)-w(t)=0\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{zz}(\tau) = \mathbb{E}[z(t)z(t-\tau)] = \mathbb{E}[(e(t)-w(t))(e(t-\tau) -w(t-\tau))] \\
= \mathbb{E}[e(t)e(t-\tau)] - \mathbb{E}[e(t)w(t-\tau)] - \mathbb{E}[w(t)...] ... \\
= R_{ee}(\tau) - R_{ew}(\tau) - R_{we}(\tau)+R_{ww}(\tau)
\end{aligned}
\]


11.2.2 3-2)
$$
\[\begin{aligned}
S_{ww}(f) = S_{yy}(f)|H(f)|^2 \\
S_{ww}(f) = (S_{ee}(f)+S_{bb}(f))|H(f)|^2

\end{aligned}\]
$$


11.2.3 3-3)
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{ew}(\tau) = R_{ee}(\tau) \ast h^*(-\tau) \\
=S_{ew}(f) = S_{ee}(f)H^*(f) \\
=S_{ew}(f) = S_{ee}(f)H(f)
=S_zz(f) = S_{ee}(f) - S_{ee}H^*(f) - S_{ee}(f)H(f) + S_{ww}(f) \\^
=S_{ee}(f)[1 - (H^*(f)+H(f)) + |H(f)|^2] ° S_{bb}(f)|H(f)|^2 \\
\end{aligned}
\] Finalement Q est:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q = \frac{S_{ee}}{S_{zz}} \\
Q = \frac{S_{ee}}{S_ee{f}[1 - 2R_e(H(f)) + |H(f)|^2 + \frac{S_bb{f}}{S_{ee}(f)}|H(f)|^2} \\
Q = \frac{1}{1 + |H(f)|^2 [1 + \frac{S_{bb}(f)}{S_{ee}(f)} -2 R_e(H(f))}
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 12  Exercice 3
text:
12.0.1 On pose \(\hat{x}(n)=ax(n-1)\). Quelle est la valeur de a qui minimise l’erreur \(P_e\) de prédiction. Calculer dans ce cas l’erreur
Soit X(n) un processus aléatoire stationnaire à l’ordre 2, de moyenne nulle et dont la fonction d’autocorrélation statistique est \(R_{xx}(\tau)\). On se propose de prédire à partir d’une observation \(x(n-1)\) la valeur de x à l’instant ultérieur n. On définit l’erreur de prédicition à l’instant n par \(e(n)=x(n) - \hat{x}(n)\),\(\hat{x}(n)=ax(n-1)\) étant la valeur prédire. L’erreur quadratique moyenne est alors \(P_e = \mathbb{E}[(x(n) - \hat{x}(n))^2]\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_e = \mathbb{E}[(x(n) - \hat{x}(n))^2] \\
= \mathbb{E}[X^2(n) - 2ax(n)x(n-1)+ a^2 x^2(n-1)]
= \mathbb{E}[x^2(n)] - 2a\mathbb{E}[x(n)x(n-1)] + a^2\mathbb{E}[x^2(n-1)] \\
P_e = R_{xx}(0) - 2aR_{xx}(1) + a^2R_{xx}(0)
\end{aligned}
\]
Quand \(P_e = 0\) on a : \[
a = \frac{R_xx(1)}{R_{xx}(0)}
\]

title: 12  Exercice 3
text:
12.1 2) Dans ce cas
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_e = R_{xx}(0) - 2 \frac{R_{xx}(1)}{R_{xx}(0)R_{xx}(1)+ (\frac{R_{xx}(1)}{R_{xx}(0)})^2R_{xx}(0)} \\
P_e = R_{xx}(0) - \frac{(R_{xx}(1))^2}{R_{xx}(0)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Modèle autorégressif
\(\hat{x}(n) = \sum^P_{i=1}a_ix(n-i)\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
e(n)=\hat{x}(n) - x(n) \\
e(n)+ax(n-1)=x(n)
\end{aligned}
\]
Random note: Réponse impulsionnelle infinie ou finie
SI y’a un retour , c’est infini comme dans ce cas.

title: 13  Kalman Filter
text:
13.1 The Kalman setup if you’re in a hurry
The Kalman filter is an extension of the Wiener filter for dynamic systems.
State vector (system state) at discrete time k: \[\mathbf{X}(k)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.\]
Process (state) evolution (linear, discrete-time with additive process noise): \[\mathbf{X}(k+1)=A\,\mathbf{X}(k)+\mathbf{W}(k),\] where A is the state transition matrix (size \(N \times N\)) and \(\mathbf{W}(k)\) is the process (system) noise.
Measurements from m sensors at time k (stacked): \[\mathbf{Y}(k)\in\mathbb{R}^{m}.\]
Linear measurement model: \[\mathbf{Y}(k)=C\,\mathbf{X}(k)+\mathbf{V}(k),\] where C is the measurement matrix (size \((M \times N)\) and \(\mathbf{V}(k)\) is the measurement noise.
If each sensor \(i\) provides scalar measurement \(y_i(k)\), then \[\mathbf{Y}(k)=\begin{bmatrix}y_1(k)\\ \vdots\\ y_m(k)\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf{V}(k)=\begin{bmatrix}v_1(k)\\ \vdots\\ v_m(k)\end{bmatrix},\qquad
C=\begin{bmatrix}c_{1}\\ \vdots\\ c_{m}\end{bmatrix}\] with rows \((C_i)\) selecting the linear combination of states observed by sensor \(i\).
Noise assumptions (white, zero-mean, uncorrelated between process and measurements):

title: 13  Kalman Filter
text:
State equation: \[
\mathbf{X}(k+1)=A\mathbf{X}(k)+\mathbf{W}(k),\quad \mathbf{W}(k)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Q).
\]
Measurement equation: \[
\mathbf{Y}(k)=C\mathbf{X}(k)+\mathbf{V}(k),\quad \mathbf{V}(k)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R)
\]
No cross-correlation: \[
(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}(k)\mathbf{V}^\top(j)]=0)\text{ for all}\quad k,j
\]
Independance between the noise and the initial state \[
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}(k){X}^T(0)] =\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{V}(k){X}^T(0)] =0\text{ for all}\quad k,j
\]

title: 13  Kalman Filter
text:
13.2 Notations and definitions

Let \(\mathbf{y}(0{:}n)=\{\mathbf{y}(0),\mathbf{y}(1),\dots,\mathbf{y}(n)\}.\)
State estimate of \(\mathbf{x}(k)\) given all measurements up to time (n): \[\hat{\mathbf{x}}(k\mid n)=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{x}(k)\mid \mathbf{y}(0{:}n)\big]\]
When \((n=k)\) this is the filtering estimate;
When \((n>k)\) this is a fixed‑lag or smoothing estimate;
When \((n<k)\) it is a prediction.
Estimation error (a random vector): \[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(k\mid n)=\mathbf{x}(k)-\hat{\mathbf{x}}(k\mid n).\]
Error covariance matrix: \[P(k\mid n)=\mathbb{E}\big[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(k\mid n)\,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(k\mid n)^{\top}\big]
=\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\mathbf{x}(k)-\hat{\mathbf{x}}(k\mid n)\big)\big(\mathbf{x}(k)-\hat{\mathbf{x}}(k\mid n)\big)^{\top}\Big].\]

title: 13  Kalman Filter
text:
13.3 Filter principle
State prediction: \[\hat{\mathbf{x}}(k+1\mid k)=A\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}(k\mid k).\]
Prediction error covariance: \[P(k+1\mid k)=\mathbb{E}\big[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(k+1\mid k)\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(k+1\mid k)^\top\big]
= A\,P(k\mid k)\,A^\top + Q.\]
Kalman gain: \[K(k+1)=P(k+1\mid k)\,C^\top\big(C\,P(k+1\mid k)\,C^\top+R\big)^{-1}.\]
Measurement update (state estimate): \[\hat{\mathbf{x}}(k+1\mid k+1)=\hat{\mathbf{x}}(k+1\mid k)+K(k+1)\big(\mathbf{y}(k+1)-C\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}(k+1\mid k)\big).\]
Measurement update (error covariance) — standard form: \[P(k+1\mid k+1)= \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}(k+1 \mid k+1)\tilde{X}^T(k+1 \mid k+1)]\]
A commonly used simplified (algebraically equivalent when K is the Kalman gain above) form is: \[P(k+1\mid k+1)=P(k+1\mid k)-K(k+1)\,C\,P(k+1\mid k).\]
To intialise the algoritihm, we need the initial state \(X(0\mid0)\) and \(P(0\mid0)\)

title: 14  Filters
text:
14.1 Convolution filter
Let \(I_s\) denote the starting (input) image, \(I_e\) the ending (output) image, and \(C_K\) the convolution kernel (filter) of size (2n+1)×(2n+1).
The discrete convolution relation at pixel (i,j) is:
\[
I_e(i,j) \;=\; \sum_{l=-n}^{n}\sum_{k=-n}^{n} C_K(k,l)\,I_s(i+k,j+l).
\]

title: 14  Filters
text:
\(I_s(i,j)\): intensity/value of the input image at coordinates (i,j).

\(I_e(i,j)\): intensity/value of the output image at coordinates (i,j) after applying the convolution.

\(C_K(k,l)\): kernel weight at offset (k,l), where k indexes columns (horizontal offset) and l indexes rows (vertical offset).

The sums run over the kernel support from -n to n in both dimensions, so the kernel size is (2n+1)×(2n+1).

Boundary handling (not shown) must be specified separately (e.g., zero-padding, symmetric extension, circular convolution).

title: 14  Filters
text:
14.2 Identity kernel

14.2.1 Formally
Let \(I_s\) be the input image, \(I_e\) the output image, and \(I_k\) the identity convolution kernel. The identity kernel is the kernel that leaves the image unchanged under convolution:
\[
I_e \;=\; I_s \ast I_k \;=\; I_s.
\]
In coordinates, for all pixels (i,j):
\[
I_s(i,j) =\sum_{l=-n}^{n}\sum_{k=-n}^{n} I_k(k,l)\,I_e(i+k,j+l) \;=\; I_e(i,j).
\] A canonical choice for \(I_k\) on a (2n+1)×(2n+1) support is the discrete delta (Kronecker) kernel:
\[
I_k(k,l) \;=\; \delta_{k,0}\,\delta_{l,0} \;=\;
\] \[
\begin{cases}
1 & (k,l)=(0,0),\\[4pt]
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
which yields the pointwise identity: \[
I_e(i,j)=\sum_{l=-n}^{n}\sum_{k=-n}^{n} \delta_{k,0}\delta_{l,0}\,I_s(i+k,j+l)=I_s(i,j).
\]

The kernel support can be larger than a single pixel; values outside the central 1 are zero.

title: 14  Filters
text:
14.3 Average (mean) filter
The average (mean) filter is a linear, shift-invariant smoothing filter that replaces each pixel by the arithmetic mean of the pixels in a local neighborhood. It reduces high-frequency noise and small-scale detail while preserving general intensity trends.
For a square window of size (2n+1)×(2n+1) the average kernel A has constant coefficients:
\[
A(k,l)=\frac{1}{(2n+1)^2},\qquad k,l\in\{-n,\dots,n\}.
\]
Convolution with the average kernel gives the output image \(I_e\) from input \(I_s\):
\[
I_e(i,j)=\sum_{l=-n}^{n}\sum_{k=-n}^{n} A(k,l)\,I_s(i+k,j+l)
= \frac{1}{(2n+1)^2}\sum_{l=-n}^{n}\sum_{k=-n}^{n} I_s(i+k,j+l).
\]

title: 14  Filters
text:
14.4 Median filter
The median filter is a nonlinear, shift-invariant denoising filter that replaces each pixel with the median of the intensities in a local neighborhood.
Given an input image \(I_s\) and a local window of size (2n+1)x(2n+1), let \(S(i,j)\) be the multiset of pixel values in that window centered at (i,j): \[
S(i,j)=\{\,I_s(i+k,j+l)\;:\;k,l\in\{-n,\dots,n\}\,\}.
\] The output pixel is the median of S(i,j): \[
I_e(i,j)=\operatorname{median}\big(S(i,j)\big).
\]

title: 14  Filters
text:
14.5 Nagao filter



Nagao filter kernel


The Nagao filter is an edge-preserving, local adaptive smoothing filter that chooses the output value from the neighborhood whose internal variance (or squared error) is minimal. It was introduced for noise reduction while preserving edges and fine details by selecting the most homogeneous local region among several oriented and shaped subwindows.

title: 15  Contour and edges
text:
15.1 Gradient filter
Horizontal and vertical gradient filters approximate first-order spatial derivatives to detect local intensity change (edges). Let I be the input image. The discrete gradients at pixel (i,j) are often computed with simple finite-difference kernels.
Definition (central differences): \[
G_x(i,j)=\frac{1}{2}\big(I(i+1,j)-I(i-1,j)\big),
\qquad
G_y(i,j)=\frac{1}{2}\big(I(i,j+1)-I(i,j-1)\big).
\] Equivalently, via convolution with 1D kernels: \[
G_x = I \ast \begin{bmatrix} -\tfrac{1}{2} & 0 & \tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix},\qquad
G_y = I \ast \begin{bmatrix} -\tfrac{1}{2} \\[4pt] 0 \\[4pt] \tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Common alternative (forward/backward differences): \[
G_x^{+}(i,j)=I(i+1,j)-I(i,j),\quad G_x^{-}(i,j)=I(i,j)-I(i-1,j),
\] and similarly for \(G_y\).
(The forward differences is the prewitt operator. If you give more importance to the value in the center,you get the Sobel operator )
Gradient magnitude and orientation: \[
M(i,j)=\sqrt{G_x(i,j)^2+G_y(i,j)^2},\qquad
\theta(i,j)=\operatorname{arctan}\big(G_y(i,j),G_x(i,j)\big).
\]
